parakeet: In many church cultures, the child role quietly invites a matching role in leadership: the father, the guardian, or the caretaker, someone who sees themselves as responsible for other adults' well-beings. Now, what the culture rehearses out loud is follower language combined with authority language. The follower language is I'm your child. I'm small. I surrender. Lead me, cover me, correct me. I'm lost. I'm nothing. I'm desperate for you. Gotta have more of you. Can't get enough of you. And yes, all of these are real lyrics from Christian songs and sermons. But then there's the authority language, which is I'm your father, your shepherd, your covering, your spiritual parent. I'm responsible for you. Obey those who have rule over you, for they care for your souls. See, this doesn't just exist in a vacuum. It finds home in scripture itself. And that's just for all of those who say, well, anybody can use it badly. Scripture itself is permission to behave badly. Now ultimately, it stops being poetic language and becomes a social script. Hierarchy starts to feel like intimacy. The relational logic that forms is because I love you, I must have authority over you. Now, this is seen widespread throughout the Bible belt in southern culture. Me expressing dominance over you, me having authority over you, me leading you, directing you, making plans for your life as the man of the house is proof that I love you. If I wasn't making plans for you, if I wasn't treating you like you're beneath me, that would be evidence that I'm not really loving you with the love of God.
